new_statements.quote: Il se peut bien bien que le langi ait des tons, mais pour l’instant il m’est impossible de dégager un système tonal, il est néanmoins claire qu’il y a un accent, qui tombe régulièrement sur la première syllabe de thème ou radical. [p. 99] … L’accent, que nous noterons par une apostrophe précédant la syllabe accentuée, se place le plus souvent sur la première syllabe du radical, il existe néanmoins quelques exceptions. En outre, les éléments grammaticaux, tels que na « avec » et ma « puis », ne portent pas d’accent. [p. 100] … Dans la grande majorité des cas, l’accent se place sur la première syllabe du thème ou du radical. Il remplit ainsi un rôle démarcatif [p. 102]
new_statements.translation: It may well be that Langi has tones, but for now I am unable to extract a tonal system; it is nevertheless clear that there is an accent, which falls regularly on the first syllable of the stem or radical. [p. 99] … The accent, which we will mark with an apostrophe before the accented syllable, is placed most often on the first syllable of the radical; there are nevertheless a few exceptions. Moreover, grammatical elements such as na 'with' and ma 'then' bear no accent. [p. 100] … In the great majority of cases the accent is placed on the first syllable of the stem or radical. It thus fulfils a demarcative role [p. 102]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two first-hand modern descriptions disagree. Dunham (2001/2005 grammar, Kondoa/Pahi speakers): a demarcative word accent (tense articulation, greater amplitude, markedly longer vowel) on the first syllable of the stem/root, i.e. the syllable after the class prefix (stem-initial = 'morphologically determined' placement); tone not established. Stegen (2002, SIL, Haubi/Kondoa/Mnenya): Rangi is a H/L tone language with the mora as TBU (nouns lexically tonal, verbs take one H on the antepenultimate stem mora spreading leftward), and the penultimate syllable 'as in many Bantu languages, normally receives stress' (p. 137). A plausible reconciliation is that Dunham's stem-initial 'accent' is the percept of Stegen's stem H tone plus lexical vowel length, while Stegen's penultimate 'stress' is Bantu penultimate lengthening; neither author tests the other's claim. Seidel 1898 (p. 388) assumes default penultimate word accent as an orthographic convention only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Dunham §5.1.2.4 (p. 102): compounds carry two accents — a weaker secondary accent on the absolute initial of the first term and the primary accent on the stem-initial syllable of the second component (mʊntʊ mʊ'ki 'woman'); reduplicated stems likewise: secondary on the first copy, primary on the second (i-,findu'findu 'tonsil'). Notation: ‘ = primary, = secondary accent (front matter, p. iv-v). Stegen 2002 says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Dunham: grammatical particles na, ma unaccented (p. 100); the locative suffix -i is always accented and H-toned (p. 100); with two prefixes the accent goes on the second prefix, treated as stem-initial (§5.1.2.2, p. 101); Swahili loans keep their penultimate accent (sa'maki, ba'hari, ra'fiki) and a set of class-9 nouns of unknown origin also have accent on C2/C3 (§5.1.2.3, p. 101), one noun attested both ways ('ŴiNgɪrɪ ~ Ŵi'Ngɪrɪ); the habitual accomplished verb form is usually pronounced with an exclamative intonation that shifts the accent from radical-initial position to the last syllable (verb chapter, cross-ref. §5.1.2). Stegen 2002 fn. 5 (p. 133): the minor Kolo dialect has lexical tonal minimal pairs on verbs which Haubi, Kondoa and Mondo dialects lack.
new_statements.domain_note: Dunham: word level, citation and text forms; duration measurements on isolated words (ma-'bahɪra 'feathers', p. 99); the swahili/langi contrast kʊpa:ta vs kupa.ta (p. 102) shows length and accent place as the cue. Stegen: p. 137 remark is made in the context of compensatory lengthening in nouns and verbs (word level); tone is treated at word and phrase level (phrase-final H deletion, pp. 132–133). Verbatim Stegen 2002: 137: 'Complementary lengthening due to prenasalized consonants applies predominantly to the penultimate position which, as in many Bantu languages, normally receives stress in Rangi.' (file, PDF p. 9). Seidel 1898: 388: 'Der Wortton ist nur dann, und zwar durch den Akut, bezeichnet, wenn er nicht auf der vorletzten Silbe ruht.'.
new_statements.identity_note: Dunham's thesis describes Langi as spoken in Kondoa town and Pahi (main informants Saidi Ikaji, Ally Ningah; Swahili-dominant urban speakers), and she calls the Kolo variety a separate dialect (p. 107). Stegen 2002 worked in Kondoa town and Mnenya village and distinguishes major dialects Haubi and Kondoa from minor Kolo and Mondo; his tone facts are for Haubi/Kondoa. Both are lang1320 (Rangi/Langi, lag); Seidel 1898 'Irangi' is the same language (Werther's Kondoa/Irangi word lists, with Mbugwe admixture noted).

readall_conflicts: The one work in scope (Stegen 2011) is silent on stress, so it adds no new conflict. The disagreement already held by the project for Rangi remains: Dunham 2001 (existing statement, §5.1.2 p. 100, verified in the on-disk text) says the accent 'tombe régulièrement sur la première syllabe de thème ou radical' (stem-initial, realized as lengthening), whereas Stegen 2002 (SAL 31, p. 137, held by the project from our earlier reading) says the penultimate position 'as in many Bantu languages, normally receives stress in Rangi', and Stegen 2002 / Gibson 2012 / Stegen 2011 all treat Rangi as a two-tone (H/L) language, with Dunham 2001 saying she could not extract a tonal system. Stem-initial (Dunham) vs penultimate (Stegen) is a genuine placement conflict between the two primary describers; Stegen 2011 does not resolve it.

sources.note: §1.1 (pp. 131–134): Rangi has H and L tones, mora is the TBU, phrase-final H deletion, nouns tonally fully distinctive, verbs get one H on the antepenultimate stem mora spreading leftward; grammatical tone. p. 137: compensatory lengthening before prenasalized consonants 'applies predominantly to the penultimate position which, as in many Bantu languages, normally receives stress in Rangi.' p. 131 mentions 'additional distinctiveness in tone and stress' in a near-minimal pair.
